<!-- Generated by R/build_report.R from report/README.Rmd. Edit the .Rmd, not this file. -->

PaleoACES compares climate-predicted and observed forest composition in Mount Rainier (MORA) and
North Cascades (NOCA) National Parks, using forest resurveys and four Holocene macrofossil records.
One CCA calibrated on the legacy survey plots provides the shared coordinate system.

This page is the supplementary appendix of the analysis. It shows every main and supplementary
figure, the tables reported in the manuscript and the modelling code, in the order of the analysis
and of the Supporting Information (Appendix S1, Appendix S2). Data cleaning is summarized by its
figure here; the step-by-step detail sits in [`report/details/`](report/details), linked from
each section.

```sh
Rscript R/run_all.R --offline   # run the whole analysis from the cached climate (add --age-models to refit Bacon)
Rscript R/build_report.R        # rebuild this page and report/ from the outputs
```

# The remodelled analysis at a glance

The Holocene side of the analysis is being remodelled on lake-periods: one lake within one climate
period, compared from its first to its last sampled century. Each row below is filled when its step
is finished.

| Step | What it does | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Step 0 | Climate variables and CCA refit | `r sprintf('MSpT + SP: VIF %.2f, adjusted R² %.3f (all four %.3f), no lake-century outside the calibration climate, display rotation %.1f°', max(read_output("cca_screening.csv")$VIF[read_output("cca_screening.csv")$set == "MSpT + SP"]), read_output("cca_screening.csv")$adjusted_R2[read_output("cca_screening.csv")$set == "MSpT + SP"][1], read_output("cca_screening.csv")$adjusted_R2[1], read_output("cca_display_rotation.csv")$angle_degrees)` |
| Step 1 | Climate periods and lake-periods | (pending) |
| Steps 2 to 4 | Mismatch, lag, turnover, pace, direction, climate change rate and fire per lake-period | (pending) |
| Step 5 | Holocene explanatory models | (pending) |
| Step 5a | Holocene against Anthropocene (era models) | (pending) |
| Step 6 | Species contributions | (pending) |

# Step 0. Climate variables and the CCA

**What and why.** The four seasonal variables come in two tightly linked pairs: spring and winter
temperature, and summer and winter precipitation. Inside a pair the CCA cannot tell the two
seasons apart, and Holocene lakes reach seasonal combinations the modern plots never show. The CCA
is therefore constrained by one variable of each pair. Spring temperature (MSpT) stands for
snowmelt timing and the start of the growing season. Summer precipitation (SP) stands for summer
drying stress. Because each pair is strongly correlated, the two also carry temperature and
precipitation change in general.

**Decisions.**

- 9 Nov 2026 (Bills, `PLAN.md` row 0): constrain the CCA by MSpT and SP, first proposed as MWT and
  SP. Rerun everything downstream. Rotate the figures only and keep every table unrotated.
- 9 Nov 2026 (taken in the run): a Holocene lake-century counts as extrapolated when its
  Mahalanobis distance from the calibration plots exceeds the 99th percentile of the plots' own
  distances, for the variables of that set. All 111 century slices of each lake's climate series
  are screened.
- 9 Nov 2026 (taken in the run): the adjusted R² of each set is vegan's permutation estimate
  (1,000 permutations, seeded). The add-back test compares the nested fits with 9,999
  permutations, unrestricted and within parks.

**Model code.**

```{r step0-code}
code_snippet('R/pipeline/10_cca.R', 'cca-fit')
```

**Result.**

```{r step0-screening}
screening = read_output('cca_screening.csv')
screening |> group_by(set) |> summarise(Variables = gsub(';', ', ', first(variables)),
    `Largest abs. correlation` = first(max_abs_correlation),
    `VIF` = paste(sprintf('%s %.1f', variable, VIF), collapse = ', '),
    `R²` = first(R2), `Adjusted R²` = first(adjusted_R2),
    `MORA lake-centuries outside (%)` = 100 * first(extrapolated_share_MORA),
    `NOCA lake-centuries outside (%)` = 100 * first(extrapolated_share_NOCA), .groups = 'drop') |>
  arrange(match(set, c('All four', 'MWT + SP', 'MSpT + SP'))) |> rename(Set = set) |>
  show_table('step0_screening', caption = sprintf(paste('**Screening of the climate constraints** on the %d',
    'legacy calibration plots. Holocene lake-centuries: %d at MORA (three lakes) and %d at NOCA.'),
    screening$n_plots[1], screening$holocene_lake_centuries_MORA[1], screening$holocene_lake_centuries_NOCA[1]))
addback = read_output('cca_screening_addback.csv')
rotation = read_output('cca_display_rotation.csv')
```

With MSpT and SP the CCA explains `r sprintf('%.1f%%', 100 * screening$adjusted_R2[screening$set == 'MSpT + SP'][1])`
of the variation in composition (adjusted R²), against
`r sprintf('%.1f%%', 100 * screening$adjusted_R2[screening$set == 'All four'][1])` with all four
variables. Adding winter temperature and winter precipitation back improves the fit
(pseudo-F `r sprintf('%.2f', addback$pseudo_F[1])`, p = `r sprintf('%.4f', addback$p_value[addback$design == 'Unrestricted'])`
unrestricted and p = `r sprintf('%.4f', addback$p_value[addback$design == 'Within parks'])` within parks).
That gain comes from the seasonal contrasts within each pair, the same contrasts that make the
four-variable fit collinear (VIF up to `r sprintf('%.1f', max(screening$VIF[screening$set == 'All four']))`)
and that place `r sprintf('%.0f%%', 100 * screening$extrapolated_share_MORA[screening$set == 'All four'][1])`
of the MORA lake-centuries outside the calibration climate. With MSpT and SP no lake-century in
either park is outside it. The display rotation turns the plane by
`r sprintf('%.1f', rotation$angle_degrees)` degrees so that rotated axis 1 is spring temperature
increasing to the right and rotated axis 2 summer precipitation increasing upward. The pipeline
asserts that mismatch, lag, turnover, pace and direction are identical before and after this rotation.

# 1. Modern vegetation

Legacy surveys and resurveys of the same plots at Mount Rainier (MORA) and North Cascades
(NOCA) National Parks were matched, cleaned and harmonized to one tree taxonomy
(`R/pipeline/01_clean_mora_vegetation.R`, `R/pipeline/02_clean_noca_vegetation.R`).

```{r fig-s1}
show_figure('report/figures/supplementary/stage_adult_seedling_past_present.pdf')
```

**Fig. S1. Tree species occurrence by developmental stage in legacy surveys and resurveys.**
Number of plots in which each species was recorded as an adult tree or seedling/regeneration at
Mount Rainier (MORA) and North Cascades (NOCA) National Parks, following taxonomic harmonization
and exclusion of understory taxa, but before applying the CCA frequency threshold. Species could
occur in both vegetation stages within the same plot. At MORA, seedlings were defined as
individuals 10–140 cm tall at both survey dates. At NOCA, however, legacy surveys classified
individuals 0–3 m tall as regeneration and those taller than 3 m as adults, whereas resurveys
recorded seedlings of 10–140 cm and adults taller than 1.4 m. Consequently, differences between
vegetation stages at NOCA should be interpreted cautiously because size-class definitions
differed between surveys.

```{r fig-s2}
show_figure('report/figures/supplementary/plots_to_cca.pdf')
```

**Fig. S2. Selection of vegetation records for canonical correspondence analysis (CCA).**
Flowchart summarizing the matching, cleaning, and selection of legacy–resurvey plots (upper
panels) and Holocene macrofossil samples (lower panels) from Mount Rainier (MORA, blue) and North
Cascades (NOCA, orange) National Parks. The final set of eligible paired plots was used both to
calibrate the CCA using legacy community composition and to assess contemporary community
change, whereas Holocene samples were projected into the fitted ordination. Plots without any
retained tree species at either survey date were excluded because they could not be assigned an
observed CCA position. Sample sizes and reasons for exclusion are indicated at each step.

# 2. Climate

Modern climate is CHELSA V2.1 monthly climate in a survey-specific window for every plot
(`R/pipeline/04_modern_climate.R`); Holocene climate is CHELSA-TraCE21k at each lake and century
(`R/pipeline/07_paleo_climate.R`).

```{r fig-s3}
show_figure('report/figures/supplementary/test_survey_year_anomaly.pdf')
```

**Fig. S3. Climate conditions and survey-specific climate windows for the Anthropocene.** Upper
panels show annual climate variation from CHELSA v2.1 (1979–2021), averaged across the paired
vegetation plots at Mount Rainier (MORA, blue) and North Cascades (NOCA, orange) National Parks.
Variables include mean annual temperature (MAT), annual precipitation (AP), and the four seasonal
seasonal variables mean spring temperature (MSpT), mean winter temperature (MWT), summer
precipitation (SP), and winter precipitation (WP); MSpT and SP constrain the CCA. Shaded areas indicate the common legacy climate
window (1979–1989). Lower panels show the six-year climate windows used for each resurvey year
(Y−5 through Y), together with the number of paired plots (n) surveyed in that year. Winter
calculations also included December of the preceding calendar year. Climate conditions were
therefore calculated separately for each plot according to its resurvey year.

```{r fig-s4}
show_figure('report/figures/supplementary/climate_holocene_timeseries.pdf', page = 2)
```

**Fig. S4. Correlations among climate variables during the Holocene and Anthropocene.** Pearson
correlation coefficients (r) were calculated across lake locations and 100-year climate intervals
for the Holocene (CHELSA-TraCE21k, left) and across vegetation plots and survey periods for the
Anthropocene (CHELSA v2.1, right). Red indicates positive correlations and blue indicates negative
correlations, with numerical values showing Pearson's r. Climate variables include mean annual
(MAT), spring (MSpT), summer (MST), and winter (MWT) temperature, and annual (AP), spring (SpP),
summer (SP), and winter (WP) precipitation. Spring corresponds to March–May, summer to June–August,
and winter to December–February.

**Choice of CCA constraints.** Candidate variables are screened by their correlations (Fig. S4)
and by their variance inflation in the fitted CCA, keeping one temperature and one precipitation
variable. With the four seasonal variables MSpT, MWT, SP and WP, the two temperatures had variance
inflation factors near 30 and opposite-signed coefficients that are not identifiable. The CCA is
therefore constrained by spring temperature, the temperature that changes most through the
Holocene, and summer precipitation. Figures in the CCA plane are rotated rigidly by the varimax
angle so that the two arrows lie along the axes; distances and angles, and therefore every
tracking metric, are unchanged by the rotation (decision of 2026-11-09 in
`r details_link('10_decisions', 'Decisions')`). The constraints of this build:

```{r cca-vif}
read_output('cca_climate_contributions.csv') |>
  transmute(Variable = variable, Label = variable_label, VIF, `CCA1 score` = CCA1, `CCA2 score` = CCA2) |>
  show_table('cca_constraint_vif', digits = 2)
```

# Appendix S1. Construction of the Holocene age–depth models

### S1.1 Why an age–depth model was required

The macrofossils are measured at known depths in a sediment core, but depth itself does not
provide an age. Sediment does not necessarily accumulate at a constant rate: for example, 1 cm of
sediment can represent relatively few years during rapid accumulation and many more years during
slow accumulation. Chronological control is available only at selected depths, through
radiocarbon dates, dated volcanic deposits, ²¹⁰Pb dating, or other independently dated horizons.
We therefore required an age–depth model to estimate the calendar age of every depth between
these dated points and, importantly, to quantify uncertainty in those estimated ages.

We used the rbacon R package, which reconstructs sediment accumulation histories within a Bayesian
framework (Blaauw & Christen 2011). Rather than drawing a single line through the dated horizons,
Bacon estimates many age–depth histories that are compatible with the chronological evidence and
assumptions about sediment accumulation. The distribution of these histories represents the
posterior chronological uncertainty shown in Fig. S5.

### S1.2 Chronological controls and radiocarbon calibration

For each core, we assembled chronological controls for which both sediment depth and age
information were available (Table S1.1). For MORA, these consisted of the core surfaces, seven
radiocarbon dates from Jay Bath and Log Wallow, dated volcanic tephra horizons, and a basal
radiocarbon age for Reflection Pond. Reflection Pond contained no radiocarbon dates of its own and
was therefore constrained by the core surface, tephra horizons, and this basal control. For
Panther Potholes, we reproduced the chronology archived in the Neotoma database using the core
surface, five ²¹⁰Pb ages, six Accelerator Mass Spectrometry (AMS) radiocarbon dates, and three
tephra horizons. We used the corrected control depths archived in Neotoma rather than the depths
reported in Prichard et al. (2009), which contain documented depth errors.

Radiocarbon ages are expressed in ¹⁴C years and cannot be treated directly as calendar ages
because atmospheric ¹⁴C concentrations have varied through time. We therefore supplied
radiocarbon ages and their laboratory errors as uncalibrated dates (cc = 1), which Bacon
calibrated against the IntCal20 Northern Hemisphere calibration curve (Reimer et al. 2020). This
converts each radiocarbon measurement into a probability distribution of plausible calendar ages.
Controls already expressed in calendar years, including the core surfaces and tephra ages, were
supplied directly (cc = 0) and were not calibrated.

The seven MORA radiocarbon ages and their laboratory errors were taken directly from Dunwiddie
(1986). For all other chronological controls, the source and interpretation of the assigned age
uncertainty are reported explicitly in Table S1.1. The Reflection Pond basal control is the mean
of the two basal radiocarbon ages of Jay Bath (QL-1704) and Log Wallow (QL-1728), 6015 ± 110 ¹⁴C yr
BP with the larger of the two laboratory errors, following P. Dunwiddie's advice that the three
basins share the same basal age (pers. comm.).

For Panther Potholes, the five ²¹⁰Pb ages were derived using a Constant Rate of Supply (CRS)
model. We retained the error values used in the archived Gavin chronology for the primary model;
however, these values correspond numerically to the ²¹⁰Pb activity uncertainties reported by
Prichard et al. (2009), rather than to independently estimated age uncertainties in years. We
therefore evaluated this uncertainty specification in a separate sensitivity analysis described
below.

```{r table-s1-1}
read_output('table_S1_1_chronological_controls.csv', col_types = readr::cols(.default = 'c')) |>
  show_table('table_S1_1_chronological_controls',
    caption = paste('**Table S1.1. Chronological controls used in the four Bayesian age–depth models.**',
      'For cc = 1, the entered age is an uncalibrated ¹⁴C age calibrated with IntCal20. For cc = 0,',
      'the entered age is already in calibrated years before present (cal yr BP; present = A.D. 1950).'))
```

### S1.3 Bayesian age–depth models

We fitted each core independently with Bacon using the settings summarized in Table S1.2. Bacon
divided each sediment core into 5-cm sections and estimated an accumulation time, in yr cm⁻¹, for
each section. Accumulation times were allowed to differ among sections but were correlated between
neighbouring sections through the model's memory parameter. The chronological controls in
Table S1.1 were then used to update these prior expectations and generate the posterior age–depth
chronology shown in Fig. S5.

The three MORA cores were modelled using the same accumulation and memory priors. Panther Potholes
instead retained the settings of the archived Bacon chronology in the Neotoma database so that our
model reproduced the published chronology while providing the complete posterior age–depth draws
required for subsequent analyses. All runs are seeded (seed 42).

```{r table-s1-2}
read_output('table_S1_2_rbacon_parameters.csv', col_types = readr::cols(.default = 'c')) |>
  show_table('table_S1_2_rbacon_parameters',
    caption = '**Table S1.2. rbacon parameters used to construct the age–depth models.**')
```

The thick volcanic deposits required one additional treatment. The MSH-Y tephra was represented as
an instantaneous depositional interval in all three MORA cores, including the 58-cm interval at Log
Wallow containing both primary and redeposited Y tephra. At Panther Potholes, the MSH-P, MSH-Y,
and Mazama tephra intervals were treated in the same way. Bacon therefore removed these intervals
while estimating gradual sediment accumulation and reinserted them without adding elapsed time.
These intervals are shown as vertical grey bands in Fig. S5.

```{r fig-s5}
show_figure('report/figures/supplementary/fig_bacon_agedepth_slump.pdf')
```

**Fig. S5. Bayesian age–depth models for the Jay Bath, Log Wallow, and Reflection Pond cores at
MORA and the Panther Potholes core at NOCA.** For each core, the three upper panels show, from left
to right, the Markov chain Monte Carlo trace, the prior (green) and posterior (grey) distributions
of sediment accumulation time, and the prior and posterior distributions of memory. In the main
panels, depth increases along the x-axis and age is expressed as calibrated years before present.
Coloured distributions at dated depths represent the chronological controls and their
uncertainty. The grey field represents the posterior distribution of possible age–depth
relationships; the central red line shows the posterior age–depth estimate and the outer dotted
lines the 95% posterior interval. Vertical grey bands identify tephra intervals treated as
instantaneous deposition.

For Panther Potholes, we reproduced the archived Neotoma chronology as the primary model. However,
Prichard et al. (2009) report uncertainties for measured ²¹⁰Pb activity, in DPM g⁻¹, and the same
numerical values were entered as age errors, in years, in the archived chronology. We therefore
fitted a sensitivity model in which the five ²¹⁰Pb controls were each assigned an assumed ±10-year
age error, all other controls and settings unchanged (Fig. S6).

```{r fig-s6}
show_figure('report/figures/supplementary/fig_bacon_pb210_sensitivity.pdf')
```

**Fig. S6. Sensitivity of the Panther Potholes age–depth chronology to uncertainty assigned to the
five ²¹⁰Pb controls in the upper 35 cm of the core.** The left panel shows that the two posterior
chronologies are nearly identical below the ²¹⁰Pb-dated section, whereas the right panel shows the
expected increase in uncertainty within the upper 35–40 cm. The uncertainty assigned to the ²¹⁰Pb
controls affects the precision of the most recent chronology but does not materially alter the
deeper Holocene chronology used in our analyses.

`r details_link('03_chronology', 'Chronology details')` (every control and its source).

# Appendix S2. Reconstruction and classification of fire histories

### S2.1 Holocene charcoal records

For MORA, we reconstructed Holocene fire activity using the Sunrise Lake, Shadow Lake, and Little
Sunrise Lake macrocharcoal records from Walsh et al. (2017). These records provide evidence of
regional fire activity on Sunrise Ridge and are independent of the Jay Bath, Log Wallow, and
Reflection Pond records used to reconstruct vegetation. For NOCA, we reconstructed Holocene fire
activity using the Panther Potholes macrocharcoal record of Prichard et al. (2009), extracted from
the archived Neotoma record and dated with the Panther Potholes chronology of Appendix S1. Thus,
at NOCA fire and vegetation records share the same core and chronology.

### S2.2 Identification of individual fire events

We reconstructed the fire-event detection analyses of Walsh et al. (2017) and Prichard et al.
(2009) within a common workflow implemented with the R package tapas
(`R/pipeline/08_fire_records.R`). CHAR was interpolated to regular intervals, its slowly varying
background estimated by robust LOWESS, and candidate fire events identified where the residual
peak component exceeded a record-specific threshold of the background noise. Candidates were
screened with a 75-year minimum-count test (p ≤ 0.05), and consecutive exceedances were treated as
one event. Record-specific settings are given in Table S2.1.

```{r table-s2-1}
events = read_output('holocene_fire_source_events.csv') |> count(lake, name = 'Accepted fire events')
read_output('holocene_fire_source_settings.csv') |>
  left_join(events, by = 'lake') |>
  transmute(Site = site, `Fire record` = if_else(lake == 'PantherPotholes', 'Panther Potholes', lake),
    `Interpolation interval (years)` = interpolation_years,
    `Background window (years)` = smoothing_years,
    `Peak threshold` = paste0(100 * threshold_probability, '%'), `Accepted fire events`) |>
  show_table('table_S2_1_fire_detection_parameters',
    caption = paste('**Table S2.1. Parameters used to reconstruct individual Holocene fire events.**',
      'All records were also screened with the same 75-year minimum-count test (p ≤ 0.05).',
      'MORA settings follow Walsh et al. (2017) and Panther Potholes settings Prichard et al. (2009),',
      'except its 12-year interpolation interval, the median resolution of our updated chronology.'))
```

```{r fig-s7}
show_figure('report/figures/worked_examples/fig_fire_event_detection_workflow.pdf', page = 2)
```

**Fig. S7. Identification of Holocene fire events in the four records.** The residual peak
component is the difference between interpolated charcoal accumulation rates (CHAR) and the
background estimated with the record's robust LOWESS window. Candidate events exceed the local
noise threshold (dashed line) and are then screened with a 75-year minimum-count test
(p ≤ 0.05): filled circles are accepted events, red crosses rejected candidates. The manuscript
example is Little Sunrise Lake (lower left; 500-year background, 95th percentile).

### S2.3 Identification of high-fire periods

We calculated fire-event frequency within centered 1,000-year windows evaluated every 100 years,
normalized each record by its own maximum, averaged the normalized MORA records wherever at least
two were available, and identified high-fire periods separately for each site with

**High-fire threshold = median + 1.4826 × MAD (Eq. 1)**

where MAD is the median absolute deviation of the normalized site-level fire-frequency series.
Consecutive above-threshold dates form one high-fire period; gaps are not bridged and no minimum
duration is imposed (`R/pipeline/11_climate_eras_high_fire.R`; worked example in
`r details_link('09_worked_examples', 'Worked examples')`).

```{r high-fire-periods}
read_output('holocene_era_high_fire_periods.csv') |>
  transmute(Site = site, `Older (cal BP)` = older_cal_bp, `Younger (cal BP)` = younger_cal_bp,
    `Duration (years)` = duration_years, `Maximum normalized frequency` = maximum_normalized_frequency,
    Threshold = threshold) |>
  show_table('high_fire_periods', digits = 2, caption = '**High-fire periods identified by Eq. 1.**')
```

### S2.4 Reproducibility against the original studies

We compared the number of events identified by tapas with those reported by Walsh et al. (2017)
and Prichard et al. (2009), and additionally reproduced the MORA analyses with CharAnalysis R
2.0.3 (Table S2.2). Event counts differed from the published values, including with CharAnalysis,
suggesting that discrepancies arise partly from differences between software implementations. We
retained tapas for one consistent detection procedure across all four records, preserving their
source-specific settings rather than tuning parameters to reproduce published counts.

```{r table-s2-2}
# Published Panther Potholes total: Prichard et al. (2009), as in the Supporting Information draft.
PRICHARD_2009_PUBLISHED_EVENTS = 59L
mora = read_output('walsh_charanalysis_software_comparison.csv') |>
  transmute(Site = 'MORA', Lake = sub(' Lake$', '', lake), Published = published_total_episodes,
    `CharAnalysis R 2.0.3` = official_r_episodes, tapas = tapas_episodes)
noca = tibble(Site = 'NOCA', Lake = 'Panther Potholes', Published = PRICHARD_2009_PUBLISHED_EVENTS,
  `CharAnalysis R 2.0.3` = NA_real_, tapas = events$`Accepted fire events`[events$lake == 'PantherPotholes'])
difference = function(t, p) sprintf('%+d (%+.0f%%)', as.integer(t - p), 100 * (t - p) / p)
rows = bind_rows(
  mora |> arrange(match(Lake, c('Sunrise', 'Shadow', 'Little Sunrise'))),
  mora |> summarise(Site = 'MORA total', Lake = '', across(c(Published, `CharAnalysis R 2.0.3`, tapas), sum)),
  noca,
  bind_rows(mora, noca) |> summarise(Site = 'Both sites', Lake = '', Published = sum(Published),
    `CharAnalysis R 2.0.3` = NA_real_, tapas = sum(tapas))) |>
  mutate(`Difference from published` = difference(tapas, Published))
show_table(rows, 'table_S2_2_fire_event_counts', digits = 0,
  caption = paste('**Table S2.2. Holocene fire-event counts reported in the original studies and',
    'reconstructed with CharAnalysis R 2.0.3 (MORA only) and tapas (all four records).**'))
```

# 4. Climate eras and high-fire periods

Holocene climate change is classified into eras of climate change and relative stability from
signed, calibration-standardized 1,000-year changes of the CCA climate variables; fire is
classified independently (S2.3). Both feed Figure 2.

```{r fig-climate-four}
show_figure('report/figures/supplementary/fig_standardized_climate_change_four_variables.pdf')
```

**Fig. S9. Holocene climate change of the four seasonal variables, climate eras and high-fire
periods.** (A) Equal-site regional median of the signed 1,000-year change of spring temperature
(MSpT), winter temperature (MWT), summer precipitation (SP) and winter precipitation (WP),
standardized by the legacy calibration standard deviation of each variable. Shading marks the
climate-change (CC) and relative-stability (S) eras, which are classified from the two CCA
constraints, MSpT and SP; filled points mark their qualifying cells (change beyond 50% of the
variable's maximum, with at least 8 of 10 phases agreeing in direction). Winter temperature and
winter precipitation are shown for context and do not define eras. Brackets at the left give each
variable's stability range. (B) Fire-frequency ratio at each park; values above 1 are high-fire
periods (Eq. 1).

```{r fig-2}
show_figure('report/figures/main/fig_standardized_climate_change_eras_fire.pdf')
```

**Figure 2. Climate eras, climate-change rates and high-fire periods** (manuscript Figure 2: the
same panels with the two CCA constraints only).

```{r era-catalog}
read_output('holocene_era_catalog.csv') |>
  transmute(Era = era_id, Class = era_class, `Older (cal BP)` = older_cal_bp,
    `Younger (cal BP)` = younger_cal_bp, `Active variables` = active_variable_directions) |>
  show_table('climate_eras', caption = '**Climate eras.**')
```

# 5. Canonical correspondence analysis

One CCA is fitted to the legacy composition of the `r cca_value('calibration_plots')` matched
plots (MORA and NOCA pooled), constrained by the climate variables above (scaling 1, Hill = FALSE).
Resurvey plots and Holocene samples are projected into it: their climate gives a predicted (LC)
position and their composition an observed (WA) position.

```{r cca-code}
code_snippet('R/pipeline/10_cca.R', 'cca-fit')
code_snippet('R/pipeline/10_cca.R', 'cca-projection')
```

```{r cca-axes}
read_output('cca_axes.csv') |>
  transmute(Axis = axis, Eigenvalue = eigenvalue, `% total inertia` = percent_total_inertia,
    `% constrained inertia` = percent_constrained_inertia) |>
  show_table('cca_axes', caption = sprintf('**CCA axes.** Constrained inertia: %.1f%% of the total.',
    as.numeric(cca_value('constrained_percent'))))
read_output('cca_anova.csv') |>
  transmute(Test = test, Component = component, df, `Pseudo-F` = pseudo_F,
    `p (unrestricted)` = p_unrestricted, `p (within parks)` = p_within_parks) |>
  show_table('cca_permutation_tests', caption = paste('**Permutation tests** (9,999 permutations,',
    'unrestricted and restricted within parks).'))
```

```{r fig-3}
show_figure('report/figures/main/fig_cca_trajectories.pdf')
```

**Figure 3. Observed and climate-predicted community trajectories** (manuscript Figure 3).

`r details_link('06_cca', 'CCA details')` (full model output, species and climate contributions,
scaling 1 against scaling 2).

# 6. Tracking metrics

For every transition (Holocene: consecutive native centuries of a lake; Anthropocene: legacy to
resurvey of a plot) the observed (WA) and climate-predicted (LC) positions give the community
displacement, the predicted displacement, the lag between them and its change, the tracking ratio
and the angle between the two directions (`R/pipeline/12_tracking.R`).

```{r tracking-code}
code_snippet('R/helpers/tracking_metrics.R', 'tracking-geometry')
code_snippet('R/helpers/tracking_metrics.R', 'tracking-corrections')
```

```{r lake-support}
read_output('cca_tracking_holocene_lake_support.csv') |>
  transmute(Site = site, Lake = lake, `Occupied centuries` = n_occupied_centuries,
    Transitions = n_transitions, `Gaps > 100 yr` = n_gaps_over_100,
    `Median duration (yr)` = duration_median, `Longest (yr)` = duration_max) |>
  show_table('holocene_lake_support', caption = '**Holocene transitions per lake.**')
```

```{r fig-sampling}
show_figure('report/figures/supplementary/fig_holocene_sampling_fire_100yr.pdf')
```

**Fig. S10. Holocene sampling support.** Macrofossil samples and accepted fire events on the native
100-year climate intervals.

`r details_link('07_tracking', 'Tracking details')` (output schema, transition displays,
species and climate contributions).

# 7. Era models

Each tracking response is compared between the Holocene and the Anthropocene with a GLS with an
era × site mean structure and era-by-site variances. Holocene transitions of a lake are
neighbours in time: the primary residual structure is MA(1) within each lake series, compared
with independent and continuous-time AR(1) residuals on identical observations.

```{r era-code}
code_snippet('R/helpers/reconstruction_models.R', 'gls-covariance')
code_snippet('R/helpers/reconstruction_models.R', 'gls-fit')
code_snippet('R/pipeline/13_era_models.R', 'era-model')
```

```{r era-contrasts}
list.files(out('era_comparison'), pattern = '^model_contrasts[.]csv$', recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE) |>
  map_dfr(readr::read_csv, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  transmute(Response = metric, Site = site, `Anthropocene − Holocene` = estimate, SE = std_error,
    `95% CI low` = conf_low, `95% CI high` = conf_high, p = p_value, Covariance = model_type) |>
  show_table('era_contrasts', caption = '**Anthropocene − Holocene contrasts by response and park.**')
```

```{r fig-4}
show_figure('report/figures/main/fig_tracking_era_distributions.pdf')
```

**Figure 4. Era contrasts, observed lag change and correction effects** (manuscript Figure 4).

The pace and direction correction effects of a transition are estimated jointly, with a paired
MA(1) structure that keeps the two effects of the same transition correlated:

```{r joint-code}
code_snippet('R/pipeline/13_era_models.R', 'joint-correction-model')
```

`r details_link('08_models', 'Model details')` (covariance comparison, coefficients, residual
checks and individual-lake checks for every response).
